sources.title: Wasauksing First Nation works to bring back wild rice — and youth are at the centre of efforts - MBC Radio
sources.evidenceText: Photo: Group photo of Wasauksing Manoomin Youth and Survey Tour on Wasauksing August 2026 Wasauksing First Nation partnered with the Anishinabek/Ontario Fisheries Resource Centre (A/OFRC) this summer to assess the health and potential of manoomin (wild rice) habitats in the community. Close up shot of manoomin (wild rice). Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland The aim of the project is to follow the community’s lead in restoring a food source that is central to Anishinaabe culture, food sovereignty and identity. In spring 2026, Wasauksing submitted a proposal to A/OFRC to support the revival of manoomin beds through scientific expertise and state-of-the-art tools while remaining grounded in the community’s own local knowledge. For Wasauksing’s Lands and Resources Office, success means more than ecological recovery — it also means “restoring personal and community well-being and self-determination; being able to manage and harvest traditional foods, strengthening our Nation’s food sovereignty.” The project aims to support the reclamation of cultural practices and traditional knowledge surrounding manoomin, while deepening community connection to land, water, and cultural identity. Through A/OFRC, Wasauksing has visited communities like Alderville to learn from Elders like Jeff Beaver, whose community has been running a wild rice reintroduction project since the 1990s. Gabrielle Perugini, A/OFRC’s lead fisheries biologist, said much of what they have learned as an organization and what makes these sort of restoration projects possible comes from knowledge keepers like Jeff Beaver from Alderville First Nation. Youth from the community spent a week alongside the A/OFRC team exploring local waters, learning the history of manoomin in their territory and getting hands-on experience with the monitoring and surveying of identified sites. “There were lots of smiles and laughing, lots of knowledge transfer and storytelling while we were out in the canoes checking in on the sites,” said Perugini. Monitoring turbidity and water quality at manoomin sites. Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland The fieldwork encouraged the youth to be part of the restoration efforts by learning how to use equipment to measure water quality at potential manoomin sites. They measured and recorded pH, turbidity, sediment composition, and water levels. They also learned to identify and document optimal growing conditions: slow-moving, clear water; lakes with inflow and outflow; depths between 0.5 and three feet; minimal water level fluctuations; and silty sediment. “I think it’s important not only from the stewardship side of things, but crucial for their spiritual connection to the land,” Perugini said of the youth’s involvement. “If you get the youth involved, they start to develop a personal relationship with the manoomin, and having some personal stake in the matter fuels their stewardship. People will protect what they love and value. The hope is that it spreads to more youth and, in the blink of an eye, you have manoomin guardians at the ready.” Gabrielle Perugini from A/OFRC teaching youth how to take soil samples. Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland While it is too early for a final report — A/OFRC still needs to compile and analyze the data — the early assessments were encouraging. Existing manoomin beds and habitats were found to be not beyond recovery, and the surveys affirmed the community’s memory of where wild rice once grew. A manoomin habitat located around Wasauksing First Nation. Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland The final survey report will be released to Wasauksing once A/OFRC has had a chance to thoroughly review and format the data after the busy summer season. The report will be kept confidential for community members and will include information on suitable wild rice habitats across various locations, insights into community participation, and plans for long-term monitoring and sustainability. Surveying the water level of a manoomin habitat near Wasauksing First Nation. Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland A project update poster is expected soon, and both organizations plan to present the work at the Wasauksing Lands and Resources Open House this spring. “Manoomin restoration goes beyond stewardship,” Perugini said. “It encourages community connectedness, strengthens food security, and fortifies spiritual and cultural connections.” For the youth who spent August surveying Wasauksing’s waters, this is just the beginning. They’ve seen what’s possible — that something lost can be brought home — and they’ve become part of a legacy that will extend far beyond their own lifetimes. “Youth bring passion with them, and it is contagious. They will be the ones with the option to continue to keep and build on that legacy,” said Neil Canvin, the natural resources co-ordinator with Wasauksing’s Lands and Resources Office. Once restoration is underway, Wasauksing plans to bring the whole community into the process. “Our desire is that, for next year and future years, we will host community events that will involve community members in the harvesting and planting processes for wild rice at the identified sites,” said Canvin. The community also plans to host workshops on the cultural dances that precede manoomin harvest and the traditional methods of processing wild rice for consumption. Manoomin (wild rice) habitat. sources.evidenceText: Copyright © 2026 Food Action Network of Northwestern Ontario For at least 7,000 years, Manomin has been cared for and cultivated by Indigenous Peoples throughout the Great Lakes watershed. Though the name “wild rice” is often used for this plant, it is misleading because it is neither wild, nor rice. It is an aquatic grass of the genus Zizania , distinct from true white rice of the genus Oryza. To label Manomin “wild” discounts the long-standing, reciprocal relationship through which Indigenous Peoples and Manomin have sustained one another. This relationship is at the heart of research partnerships between multiple Indigenous communities, including Obishikokaang (Lac Seul), Alderville and Mississauga First Nations and our Lakehead University team from Anthropology, Geography, and Health Sciences. Together, we aim to create a network for communities to share knowledge and practices to restore Manomin. Among many Anishinaabeg communities, Manomin is known as the Good Berry, a name that speaks to more than nourishment alone. Historically, it has sustained communities, due to its many nutritional benefits. Traditional harvesting practices are grounded in sustainability, with care being taken to avoid overharvesting. Many communities hold the teaching that one third of the harvest is gathered for food, one third is left for waterfowl and other relations, and the remainder returns to the water to re-seed the plant. However, colonial policies and industrial development in the Great Lakes region have disrupted this balance. Changing water levels and the introduction of pollutants have affected Manomin health, diminished vitality of plants and limited community access to this culturally significant food. For example, in Obishikokaang, the construction of a hydroelectric dam in the 1930s raised water levels in Lac Seul and destroyed thousands of acres of Manomin beds. Our Lakehead University team aims to support Indigenous partners as they restore plant beds and renew relationships between people and Manomin. In this work, Manomin is not treated as an object of study, but as a relational being that guides ecological restoration and the renewal of community knowledge. We are committed to strengthening Indigenous food sovereignty by supporting gatherings for people to learn more about the revitalization of this culturally significant grain and training students whose projects help to address research questions about Manomin. During the recent Manominike-Giizis (Manomin harvesting moon), in late August through September, we had the privilege of participating in harvesting and processing gatherings. Together with Obishikokaang Elders, Knowledge Holders, and other community members, we travelled to the shores of Lake Huron to Mississauga First Nation. Participants brought with them Manomin harvested from five different areas to be processed together using traditional methods to transform the harvested plant into edible grains. As pictured, the first step is to roast the plant over a fire in a large kettle. Next, the Manomin is placed into a lined pit in the ground, and gently danced upon while wearing new moccasins to separate the grain from the chaff. Lastly, it is tossed from a birch bark basket into the air, often over a blanket, to winnow the chaff from the edible portion. These steps in Manomin preparation foster a cooperative environment that incorporates cultural traditions, the sharing of food and builds strong community bonds. The experience deepened our understanding of this labour of love required to nourish communities through traditional foodways. We enjoyed a variety of dishes, including Manomin soup with turkey sausage, cold Manomin sweetened with maple syrup and raspberries, and crispy Manomin egg fritters. Manomin revitalization is not simply about restoring a food source, but about honouring Indigenous sovereignty, repairing Anishinaabe relationships with the land and water, and listening to the teachings of the Good Berry itself. To learn more, please watch the short video “Manomin Dreams: The Restoration of Wild Rice at Lac Seul First Nation” ( https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MXgQm9h-qmE&t=3s ). results.headline: Four candidates, four visions: How Mississauga’s mayoral hopefuls would tackle affordability, housing, crime and transit | The Pointer

sources.title: Four candidates, four visions: How Mississauga’s mayoral hopefuls would tackle affordability, housing, crime and transit
sources.evidenceText: With the increased powers mayors across Ontario hold, the decision to elect a new one carries immense weight for each of Mississauga’s 800,000-plus residents. Mississauga’s next mayor will inherit a city at a crossroads, where the cost of living is climbing, housing remains out of reach for the vast majority and growing congestion is testing the limits of local infrastructure. Unique, complex dynamics have also forced crime to the top of the City Hall agenda. Four front-running candidates, each with varying amounts of political experience, believe they can take on the challenge of leading one of Canada’s largest, fastest-growing cities. Alvin Tedjo has served Ward 2 as a councillor during the council term now drawing to a close, and was joined by Dipika Damerla who has represented Ward 7. Both ran in the 2024 mayoral by-election against Carolyn Parrish, who was victorious and is now seeking re-election after serving as mayor for two years. The three current members of council are joined by Bonnie Crombie , who is running again after taking over the leadership of the Ontario Liberals following just over nine years as Mississauga’s mayor. Tedjo has almost four years of experience representing constituents as an elected official, all at the council level; Damerla has been on council for almost eight years and served as an MPP representing Mississauga for seven years prior to that. Both Parrish and Crombie were Mississauga MPs; they both served as the Ward 5 councillor and both have been mayor. All four of the front-running candidates (The Pointer is not featuring other mayoral candidates who are far behind in the race according to public polling) are prioritizing affordability, crime and transportation (moving residents across the city and the GTA). In addition, Damerla has also made accountability inside City Hall a main focus of her campaign. Their proposed solutions to the challenges Mississauga residents face offer voters contrasting visions, from how they would control crippling property taxes and create badly needed affordable housing in the booming city, to how certain types of crime plaguing communities should be confronted while not allowing police spending to break the backs of homeowners, and managing major transit and transportation projects to ease the city’s rapidly worsening congestion. While all four candidates recognize that affordability, housing, crime and transportation are critical issues—the priorities voters are focused on as they decide who will get their vote on October 26—the candidates are proposing different solutions to confront the most pressing problems. A Mainstreet Research poll, commissioned by Y Media, conducted at the end of September showed Bonnie Crombie was the top choice of voters for Mississauga mayor, but other candidates are only slightly behind her. (Mainstreet Research) A poll conducted by Liaison Strategies at around the same time also found Bonnie Crombie is leading Carolyn Parrish by a narrow margin with Alvin Tedjo not far behind. (Liaison Strategies) Property taxes emerged as one of the defining issues in recent debates over the past two weeks, with candidates pitching their promises to freeze taxes for differing periods, limit increases to the inflation rate, or find more creative ways to expand the budget at an affordable rate by finding significant savings through external financial oversight—Damerla has been pushing for this during the council term, but Parrish and Tedjo shot down her motion for an independent Mississauga auditor general role earlier in the year. Tedjo wants to freeze the City portion of property taxes (Mississauga’s amount gets blended with the Region of Peel property tax increase to establish the total amount) for two years. “I’m committed to freezing property taxes for every single family in this city for the next two years to make sure that people have the ability to live in their homes with dignity and not have to make the choice between groceries or taxes,” he said during the Food Banks debate. “This is the single biggest tool that the City of Mississauga has at its disposal. It’s the property tax rate.” His promised freeze typically ends up badly for taxpayers, who still see large increases from spending that is shifted to the Region, onto utility bills or, in some cases, to a range of user fees. Debt financing or clawing funds from reserve accounts meant for emergencies and critical needs are options to offset tax freezes, but also have dire consequences for taxpayers immediately after budget cuts are made to achieve a freeze. North of Mississauga, Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown, when campaigning in 2018, championed freezing property taxes. The end result of years of successive tax freezes has seen some of the City’s most critical projects left behind , as projects like the Riverwalk flood mitigation plan, the downtown redevelopment project, a promised stadium Brown vowed to build, a tunnelled LRT into Brampton’s city centre, its first standalone university, a second hospital which requires a City Hall funding contribution, fire facility upgrades, transit infrastructure needs bottlenecking the system, have been shelved, delayed, or continuously underfunded. City Hall’s costs to homeowners, meanwhile, pushed a record amount of properties into tax arrears due to Brown’s failed fiscal planning . Freezing property taxes typically causes a “pay-for-it-later” crisis, when the price to catch up with delayed costs to run and maintain a city ends up being far greater in the immediate future. Tedjo is promising to allow eligible senior homeowners to defer property tax payments altogether until they sell their homes, when the amount owing would be recouped. He stumbled badly when peppered with questions and suggestions that his pitch is nothing more than an election stunt that would never get approved, and he could not explain how the deferral would work or how a range of practical problems with his idea would be addressed. sources.evidenceText: Fact-checked biographies and platform summaries for all the candidates for mayor of Mississauga. There are 14 candidates running in a crowded race for mayor of Mississauga. Incumbent Carolyn Parrish faces off against former mayor Bonnie Crombie in a close race, with councillors Alvin Tedjo and Dipika Damerla also drawing notable support in polls. Candidate Tracker was first published on October 5, 2026. Updates to candidates’ bios and platforms will be made intermittently and dated. We will add school trustees in the coming weeks. Candidate Tracker was researched, written, and verified by The Local’s team of journalists and fact checkers. Biography: Bonnie Crombie is the former three-term mayor of Mississauga, serving from 2014 to 2024. She resigned in January of that year to lead the Ontario Liberals. She subsequently stepped down from Liberal leadership early this year, after the party came third behind Premier Doug Ford’s Conservatives and the NDP in the 2025 Ontario election, and after Crombie failed to win a seat in Mississauga East–Cooksville. Before serving in these roles, Crombie was Liberal MP for Mississauga-Streetsville from 2008 to 2011, and before that worked in business. She has described herself as centrist, fiscally conservative, and socially liberal. As mayor, she advocated for Mississauga to separate from Peel Region, which she said would allow Mississauga’s tax dollars to stay in the city. On housing, she used her strong mayor powers to allow four-plexes to be built on low-rise residential lots, arguing the move would ease the housing crisis. Under her leadership the City of Mississauga signed a deal with the federal government to provide nearly $113 million for housing in Mississauga. However, council still faced criticism from some for its aversion to highrise developments under Crombie, and for rejecting more housing development applications than it accepted in 2023, according to Mississauga News. Crombie fought the Ford government’s use of minister’s zoning orders or MZOs to force high-rise developments in Mississauga that were not supported by city planners. Crombie’s 2024 budget included a residential tax increase that would go towards increased bus services in Mississauga, among other budget items. Crombie also supported expanded transit in the city and is in favour of increased urban density and a reduced reliance on cars in Mississauga. During her provincial leadership campaign, criticized the government of Kathleen Wynne for spending too much money on health care, dental care, and child care, and argued these costs should be covered by the federal government rather than the province. However, she has also described health care and education as underfunded by Ford. Platform: Crombie says Mississauga is struggling with a high cost of living, crime, and a slow-moving municipal government. According to Mississauga publication The Pointer, she wants to reduce city hall departmental spending by 10 percent in her first two years due to “out of control” spending by the city. She aims to keep taxes low. Like her rival candidate Carolyn Parrish, Crombie says Peel Region’s police funding formula needs to change, but she says she is more supportive of police than Parrish, and criticized the sitting mayor for departing the police board over the growth of the force’s budget. On tariffs, Crombie says she will let businesses that are directly affected defer their property taxes to the city without interest, and make Buy Canadian and Made-in-Mississauga procurement processes permanent. She says she’ll create a tariff response team that will respond within 48 hours to major employers facing significant decisions, and will attract investment to the industrial employment zone around Pearson airport and to the Lake Ontario waterfront. Biography: Carolyn Parrish is the current mayor of Mississauga and a former MP for Mississauga-Erindale, where she has sat as both a Liberal and independent. As mayor, she made transit free for seniors, veterans and members of the military, and created a free fitness and recreation pass for seniors. On housing, earlier this year, Parrish successfully motioned for the elimination of development charges for 1.5- and two-bedroom apartments in the city; the Mayor’s Housing Task Force has worked to increase the number of permits to develop new housing. She used “strong mayor powers,” implemented by Ford, to fire and hire top city staff—a move that the terminated city manager said risked “politicizing the bureaucracy.” She resigned from the Peel Police Services Board in 2024, over a 21.3 percent budget increase for police, saying she could not condone the hike while people struggled to afford food and housing. Parrish fought for Brampton to pay more towards the Peel police force, arguing that Mississauga contributes more money when it actually has a smaller population. (The population of Brampton surpassed that of Mississauga for the first time last year.) In a 2024 letter addressed to Minister Calandra, Parrish wrote that Mississauga pays 62 percent of the Peel police budget, while Brampton pays 38 percent. Parrish has developed a reputation for bluntness. According to The Pointer , through the course of her career, she was vocally opposed to the U.S. war in Iraq, and showed support for Palestine. More recently, after the city drew criticism for raising a Palestinian flag and then planned to raise an Israeli flag, Parrish moved a motion banning the raising of any flags besides Canada’s at Celebration Square. sources.evidenceText: Mississauga’s top mayoral candidates face off in 1st debate Four Mississauga mayoral candidates faced off in the first election debate of the campaign on Friday. Presented in partnership by the Mississauga Board of Trade and CBC News, the debate was hosted by CBC Peel's Nav Nanwa at Sheridan College's Hazel McCallion Campus. Polling last month placed Mayor Carolyn Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie neck and neck with 35 per cent support among decided voters. The Liaison Strategies poll suggested Coun. Dipika Damerla would receive 13 per cent of the vote, and Coun. Alvin Tedjo would get nine per cent. With just over a month left until election night, the candidates didn't hesitate to fire at each other's platforms. Here are the top three moments from the debate. The four candidates agreed that the current regional funding formula for policing means Mississauga is investing more than what it gets in return. Earlier this year, Parrish said the city is spending more money on regional policing than Brampton, despite Brampton having a larger population, and threatened to create Mississauga's own police force if the funding formula doesn't change. It's not the first time Parrish has spoken out against police funding. She resigned from the Peel Police Service Board two years ago after opposing a large increase to its budget. Mississauga Mayor Carolyn Parrish resigns from Peel Police Service Board in light of 21.3% budget increase But at Friday’s debate, Crombie and Tedjo argued that the mayor of Mississauga should be at the police board advocating for the city and a more equal funding formula. Four Mississauga mayoral candidates faced off in the first election debate of the campaign on Friday at Sheridan College's Hazel McCallion Campus. From left to right: CBC Peel host Nav Nanwa, Carolyn Parrish, Bonnie Crombie, Deepika Damerla and Alvin Tedjo, (Tony Fera/CBC) "That's your job. It's your responsibility to fight for Mississauga, for negotiation, to go for Mississauga and make sure that the right resources and the right budget are passed at the police board," Tedjo said. "You have abdicated not only the police board, but your duties, your fiduciary duty as mayor," Crombie said. Parrish said the police board is an arms-length institution and she can't criticize the board while serving on it. City council recently agreed to put a moratorium on the development of data centres to give time for public consultation and to explore guardrails as public concerns grew. Mississauga city council votes to block data centre projects for 1 year Parrish called the moratorium a response to public reaction and said data centres need to exist in Mississauga to attract major companies. She added that the city needs to proceed carefully and slowly to establish data centres in a safe and comfortable way. Mayor Carolyn Parrish says data centres will attract companies like Astrazeneca to Mississauga and create room for other growing industries. (Tony Fera/CBC) Tedjo raised concerns over granting limited, developable lands to American companies, while Crombie said the city needs to reconsider if it's the best use of the land. None of the candidates offered an alternative solution or said they would outright ban datacentres. The two city councillors running for mayor got to square up against each other as well. Tedjo took the opportunity early on in the debate to flex his recent historic endorsement from the Peel Regional Police Association. He said the police union endorsed him because it understands his plan to keep the community safe, which includes plans for more mental health professionals and crisis workers responding to calls. But Damerla took aim at Tedjo's track record of supporting police budget increases. She specifically pointed to 2025, when Tedjo was one of three Mississauga city councillors on Peel Region council to vote for a 23.3 per cent police budget increase , the largest in the region's history. Alvin Tedjo flexed his historic mayoral-endorsement from the Peel Regional Police Association. (Tony Fera/CBC) "Alvin did not even try and fight for a fairer police budget. You talk about [how] you're going to stand up for residents, 'Oh, taxes have gone up 30 per cent,'" Damerla challenged. Tedjo pointed out he initially supported a motion to revise the budget increase. "We all wanted to make sure that what was being proposed was fair. We wanted them to reconsider it. I also voted to send it back," Tedjo said. Peel council tells police to lower 2025 budget request, says it's 'not sustainable' The mayoral candidates are set to meet again Thursday for the next mayoral debate presented by Food Banks Mississauga and Metamorphosis Network, a group of non-profit organizations. sources.evidenceText: In the run-up to this month’s municipal election, the Star is profiling several key battleground races, offering intimate portraits of the candidates and the issues moving voters. In today’s spotlight is Mississauga. The Mississauga mayoral race has been a winding Shakespearean tale featuring a 15-year rivalry, a possibly hubristic return, a debate stage duel, the sudden emergence of a dark horse and the looming presence of a ghost. There is incumbent Carolyn Parrish, who realized her decades-old dream of becoming mayor when then-mayor Bonnie Crombie quit to become Ontario Liberal leader. There is Crombie, who succeeded the inimitable Hazel McCallion after her 36-year tenure, won her third mayoral election in a landslide and is invoking McCallion’s name to do so again in a high-stakes comeback following her failed bid to oust Premier Doug Ford. Start your Independent Membership today. A prized second-century artwork from the famed Fayoum portraits, known as the "Tondo of the Two Brothers", was unveiled following restoration in Egypt on Sunday. Specialists from Rome worked alongside conservators at the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir — where the collection is typically housed — for three weeks to restore the piece, officials announced at a press conference. Fayoum mummy portraits were created primarily on thin wooden panels and placed over the faces of the dead inside mummy wrappings, merging Egyptian funerary traditions with wider Greco-Roman artistic influences. Egypt is set to lend a significant portion of the collection to a temporary exhibition in Rome, marking the first time it will travel abroad. “The restoration of the Tondo of the Two Brothers is an important example of what can be achieved through international cooperation in the preservation and study of cultural heritage,” said Sherif Fathy, Egypt’s minister of tourism and antiquities. “Egypt and Italy share deep historical and cultural ties, and this project brings together Egyptian and Italian expertise to preserve an exceptional work of art for future generations.” Experts describe the painting as unusual because of its circular shape and its depiction of two people instead of one, and rank it among the most vivid surviving portraits from Roman-era Egypt. It was painted using a technique in which pigments are mixed with molten wax, and restorers were able to recover the features of the brother on the right. Aly Abdel Halim, director general of the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir, said the conservation required careful intervention because both the wooden support, damaged by termites, and the painted surface were fragile. The portraits will be featured in an exhibition in Rome from November to May 2027. Tomaso Radaelli, chairman of MondoMostre, the exhibition’s organizer, said it will bring together more than 110 objects, including painted panels, funerary shrouds, masks, marble portraits, plaster casts and ancient jewelry.

sources.evidenceText: Ghana's preferred news source: Accurate, Credible, Objective, Timely Kumasi, Sept. 02, GNA – In a modest conference room at the Doxa Court Hotel in Bolgatanga, 21 people from two countries sat down to confront a problem that respects no border: a river that has, for years, brought both life and devastation to the communities along its banks. The White Volta, known in Burkina Faso as the Nakambé, begins its journey from the north of the border and flows into Ghana, carrying with it not just water, but risk. When Burkina Faso’s Bagre Dam releases excess water, the surge travels downstream into Ghana’s Upper East, North East and Northern Regions, often with little warning. The result? Villages flood, farms destroyed, lives lost. The meeting, convened under the Adaptation and Vulnerability-Strengthening Trans-disciplinary Engagement for Climate Resilience (AV-STEC) project, brought together scientists, government officials, disaster management officers and traditional authority representatives from Ghana and Burkina Faso to ask a hard question: after years of goodwill and good intentions, why does the warning system still fail the people who need it most ? Since 1999, the annual release of excess water from Burkina Faso’s Bagre Dam, commissioned in 1992, has battered communities downstream in Ghana. Under the pressure of erratic rainfall and a changing climate, what was a necessary safety measure for the dam has become an increasingly, destructive annual ritual. The overflow from the White Volta floods more than two dozen districts across several regions each year, wrecking farmland and infrastructure and displacing thousands. The project is jointly implemented by the Centre for Biodiversity Conservation Research (CBCR) in Ghana and Naturama in Burkina Faso, in partnership with York University in Canada and the START International/Stolkholm Environment Institute. It combines nature-based solutions, vulnerability assessments, improved localised climate information and stakeholder engagement to build resilience in flood-prone communities on both sides of the border. The project is funded through the Climate Adaptation and Resilience (CLARE) Initiative, supported by Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC). The Bolgatanga meeting itself grew out of that mandate, a recommendation from AV-STEC’s technical research teams that policymakers from both countries needed to work together. The scientific presentations set an urgent tone. Climate projections shared at the meeting suggest Northern Ghana’s future will not simply be wetter or drier, but hotter, more unpredictable, and more prone to compounding disasters. Hydrological modelling of the Nakambé watershed pointed to an intensification of floods and droughts alike in the coming decades, particularly under high-emissions climate scenarios. Socio-economic research presented at the gathering added a human face to the data: households headed by people aged 60 and above were found to be disproportionately vulnerable to climate shocks, a finding that speaks to the elderly farmers and grandparents who often bear the heaviest burden when floodwaters rise with little notice. If there was a single thread running through the day’s discussions, it was this: the technology and science to predict floods exist, but the information often does not reach the people living along the water path in time. Participants, working in English and Francophone groups, mapped out the issues in painstaking detail. District assemblies lack transport and fuel to physically reach remote communities. Agencies holding forecast data do not always talk to the disaster responders on the ground, and even when warnings do arrive, some communities have grown weary of false alarms and ignore them – a dangerous complacency in a region where the next flood could be the worst yet. On the Burkina Faso side, the group’s diagnosis was sharper still: unchecked settlement along the riverbanks, weak coordination between institutions, and populations that have not been brought fully into flood preparedness planning. The proposed remedies were practical rather than grand — better-resourced community information centres, trained disaster volunteers, WhatsApp and SMS alert systems, more weather stations, and stronger enforcement against communities settling in flood-prone buffer zones. But perhaps the most consequential conversation of the day happened after the group work ended, when talk turned to the machinery of cooperation itself. Mr. Ernest Sanou, Chief Hydrologist at Burkina Faso’s national utility SONABEL, revealed a telling gap: letters seeking closer coordination with Ghana’s Volta River Authority, sent as far back as October 2025, had gone unanswered. It was a small but pointed illustration of how trans-boundary cooperation can stall — not for lack of will at the community level, but for lack of a reliable channels at the top. Participants converged on a solution that had eluded the two countries for years: a formal “Bagre-Kompienga Release Protocol”, built on real-time data sharing and pre-agreed spill thresholds, so that a release upstream triggers an automatic, predictable chain of warnings downstream, rather than a scramble after the water is already moving. Mr. Cedric Dzelu, representing Ghana’s Minister of State for Climate Change and Sustainability, committed to briefing the Minister with a recommendation to convene a high-level ministerial meeting between the two countries that will commit to sustain political momentum. Ms. Tiaho Cecile of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Burkina Faso, confirmed her country’s Water Minister was equally invested, noting that bilateral engagements had already taken place in October 2025 and February 2026. Dr. Atanga explained that Ghana has a legitimate basis to engage Burkina Faso through the Volta Basin Authority, whose charter promotes cooperation among member states in the equitable and sustainable management of the Volta River Basin. sources.evidenceText: Submerged trees in the catchment area of the Ken River near the Majhgawan Dam in Ajaygarh, Madhya Pradesh state, on Sept 20. AJAYGARH, India – Standing knee-deep in the Ken River, with mud smeared on her face to symbolise a connection to land her family has farmed for more than a century, Bitti Bai Kondar is among hundreds of tribal residents voicing anger over an US$87 billion (S$111 billion) government project to link India’s rivers. The mother of four adult sons, who are all protesting with her, has watched as rising water from work on the project has flooded her village. But the protesters say they would rather die than leave their ancestral home without better compensation. “The government is taking our land and water without giving us another place to live,” said Kondar, who is among scores of women who have shown their defiance by lying on mock funeral pyres. “They’re digging up our soil to build their dam, but they’re not giving us enough compensation to rebuild our lives.” The dispute is an early test for India’s ambitious plan to link some 30 rivers nationwide, which has been decades in the making but gathered momentum only in recent years, championed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The aim is to redistribute water to drought-prone regions, boosting food security by aiding tens of millions of farmers in a country where agriculture remains a major employer. Critics say the programme risks uprooting communities and damaging fragile ecosystems. Connecting Madhya Pradesh state’s Ken River to Uttar Pradesh state’s Betwa River is phase one, with a cost of about US$4.6 billion. The government has offered residents along the Ken River in Panna district, Madhya Pradesh, at least 1.25 million Indian rupees (S$16,500) a hectare, more than double the initial offer of 500,000 rupees. Usha Parmar, the district administrator, said compensation to over 90% of people had already been paid. However, some residents argue that the payments do not cover all their losses. Dhaniram Bhatnagar, a local priest, said the temple where he worked had been completely submerged. “The temple was my only source of income and now it is gone,” he said. “The compensation offered by the government is only for my home, and that is not enough.” Environmentalists have long opposed the project, saying the proposed 2km-long Daudhan Dam on the Ken River will inundate some 9,000ha of land, including a significant portion of the Panna Tiger Reserve, one of India’s most successful tiger conservation programmes. The government has said the environmental impact is “unavoidable”, but can be mitigated through tree planting, wildlife conservation and other measures. Some critics even question the scientific basis for the multibillion-dollar plan. “There is a big question mark over this project’s feasibility because it rests on a hydrological presumption: a surplus in the Ken basin and a deficit in the Betwa basin,” said Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People. “That presumption has never been conclusively established.” A government spokeswoman said she could not immediately comment on the scientific assumptions underpinning the project and referred Reuters to an Aug 21 statement that said the project would help address chronic water scarcity in the Bundelkhand region, providing irrigation, drinking water and hydropower. Around noon, on October 6, a group of women and men gather under an old banyan tree next to a water catchment area in Banhari Kalan village of Madhya Pradesh’s Panna district. After a brief meeting, they pick up their green and yellow flags and handmade posters on cardboard. The women enter the water, while the men begin sloganeering on the shore. Some elderly women lie on symbolic pyres in the water, and others stand with loose nooses around their necks, while a man is strapped to a cross. The chanting begins with slogans like “ Nyaay do ya maar do (Give us justice or kill us); Ladenge aur jeetenge (We will fight and win);” and “ Hum apna adhikar maangte, nahi kisi se bheekh maangte (We demand our right, not alms from anyone).” The methods of protest are chita andolan (pyre agitation) and jal satyagraha (water resistance). This has become part of people’s routines here. They gather at the spot twice a day to keep a protest alive, while carrying on with their daily lives. The protest was launched on September 11 against a dam being built under the Majhgaon Medium Irrigation Project of the Madhya Pradesh government. This will displace 1,450 families in four villages out of eight in the Ajaygarh sub-division. The project requires 1,552 hectares of land across eight villages, of which 988 hectares are privately owned. This land has been acquired by the Madhya Pradesh government. Villagers, mostly tribals, have demands involving fair compensation and rehabilitation. The project will cost ₹693 crore. The protestors allege irregularities, inconsistencies, and delays in the compensation process, despite the land acquisition having begun in 2018. The project will benefit 43 villages, irrigate 8,370 hectares of land, and help with drinking water in the area, according to government documents. Closing in on a month, the movement currently survives without its leaders, Amit Bhatnagar and Divya Ahirwar of the Jai Kisan Sangathan, a farmer-led movement. While Ahirwar is currently lodged in Panna district jail, Bhatnagar has been granted bail but has been sent to neighbouring Rewa for treatment following a seven-day hunger strike. While demonstrations have been going on in villages for about two years, they gained national attention in April, 2026, when Bhatnagar, a Chhatarpur-based activist, brought together people being affected by five projects and launched a jal satyagraha on the banks of the Barana river near Kupi village. The projects included the ₹44,000 crore ambitious Ken-Betwa River Link Project (KBLP) of the Union Government, the Madhya Pradesh Government’s Barethi Solar Power Project in Chhatarpur, and Majhgaon and Runjh medium irrigation projects in Panna. Despite the improvement, interest obligations continued to exceed the government’s total revenue, leaving limited resources for infrastructure, public services and other expenditure commitments. According to the report, Federal Government revenue increased by N2.6tn, or 72.2 per cent, from N3.6tn in the first half of 2025 to N6.2tn in the corresponding period of 2026. sources.evidenceText: Interest payments on public debt are exceeding government spending on health and/or education in nearly four-fifths of sub-Saharan African countries, raising concerns about the resources available to fund schools, improve learning conditions and expand access to quality education. The World Bank disclosed this in its October 2026 Africa Economic Update, noting that rising debt-servicing costs continue to place pressure on government finances across the region. According to the report, interest payments averaged between 2.9 and 3.2 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) across sub-Saharan Africa between 2023 and 2026, limiting the funds available for essential public services, including education. The development highlights the financial challenges facing governments as they seek to improve educational infrastructure, recruit and retain teachers, and provide learning materials amid competing budgetary demands. The World Bank said the region’s overall fiscal deficit is projected to decline from 5.6 per cent of GDP in 2020 to 3.5 per cent in 2026. It also projected a further reduction to an average of 3.1 per cent in 2027 and 2028. Despite the improving fiscal outlook, the report warned that high interest payments continue to restrict government spending on other priorities. “In nearly four-fifths of the countries in the region, interest payments exceed public spending on health and/or education,” the report stated. Government revenue is projected to increase by 2.6 percentage points of GDP between 2024 and 2026, compared with a projected 2.3-percentage-point increase in total expenditure. However, only 0.4 percentage point of the increase in spending is expected to come from non-interest expenditure, limiting the scope for expanding public services. For the education sector, this raises concerns about governments’ capacity to increase investment in school infrastructure, teacher development, educational technology and programmes aimed at improving access to learning. The World Bank noted that the debt challenge in sub-Saharan Africa is increasingly defined by the cost of servicing existing obligations rather than simply the accumulation of additional borrowing. The report said the median country in the region entered 2025 with general government gross debt equivalent to 57 per cent of GDP, nearly double the 29 per cent recorded in 2012. Although debt ratios have declined modestly from their 2023 peak of 60 per cent of GDP, the apparent stabilisation masks differences between countries and a deterioration in the structure of public debt. Domestic borrowing has become the dominant source of government financing since 2021, accounting for more than half of total public debt. However, domestic debt typically carries higher interest rates and shorter repayment periods than concessional external financing, exposing governments to greater refinancing pressures. The report warned that debt-service obligations are absorbing a larger share of public revenue, reducing the fiscal space available for infrastructure, human capital development and social protection. “Crowding out productive expenditure can slow capital accumulation, weaken productivity growth, and hinder poverty reduction,” the report stated. Education, as a key component of human capital development, remains vulnerable when governments have fewer resources to invest in schools, teachers and learning opportunities. Nigeria’s debt-servicing costs provide a national perspective on the World Bank’s findings, as rising interest payments compete with other public spending priorities, including education and healthcare. According to a Nairametrics analysis of Debt Management Office data, Nigeria spent approximately ₦16 trillion servicing its debt in 2025, representing a 22.9 per cent increase from ₦13.02 trillion in 2024. A separate Nairametrics report in August 2026 stated that Nigeria incurred ₦10.61 trillion in additional debt-service costs between June 2023 and December 2025, exceeding the ₦6.47 trillion spent on strategic infrastructure development over the same period. Nigeria further spent ₦3.14 trillion servicing domestic debt in the first quarter of 2026, a 20.3 per cent increase from the corresponding period in 2025, according to the report. The World Bank’s findings highlight the need for African governments to balance debt obligations with sustained investment in essential public services. For education, the challenge extends beyond allocating funds to ensuring that available resources translate into better-equipped classrooms, adequate teaching personnel, improved learning outcomes and wider access to quality schooling. As governments contend with rising financing costs, the ability to protect education budgets will remain important to efforts to strengthen human capital, reduce poverty and expand opportunities for young people across the region. sources.title: China's debt interest costs are soaring above U.S. levels and growing faster than any other budget category as Beijing struggles to prop up growth | Fortune
sources.imageAlt: China's President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan stand together as they arrive with US President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump to visit the National Archives in Washington, DC on September 25, 2026.
sources.evidenceText: The world is flooded with debt, but while the U.S. and Europe have caused angst on global markets lately, China’s fiscal situation isn’t looking so great either. In fact, China’s debt has shot up so much in recent years that interest payments on all its borrowing are commanding a bigger share of public spending. Debt-servicing payments will account for 19.2% of the central government’s general public budget this year, up from 12% in 2014, according to new Conference Board estimates cited by the Financial Times . That tracks with a separate report earlier this year from the Center for Strategic and International Studies , which also found that 19% of Beijing’s spending is earmarked for interest on debt. That’s more than the 14% of the U.S. federal budget that goes to interest costs, though less than Japan’s 25.6%. CSIS added that China’s spending on interest payments skyrocketed 341% between 2013 and 2025, faster than any other major budget category. By comparison, total spending jumped 102% in that span, with outlays on social security and employment up 207%, science and technology up 137%, and defense up 141%. To be sure, U.S. debt-interest spending looks grim too and has surged about 390% since 2013 to $1 trillion, which also tops the Pentagon’s budget. But the world’s two biggest economies have been diverging in key ways with implications for future growth and indebtedness. The U.S. economy is accelerating, helped by the AI boom, and despite high inflation, resilient consumers have continued to spend. Unemployment is low and signals full employment, while stock markets are at or near record highs. Of course, hyperscalers are racing to issue bonds to fund their data centers and chip purchases, but they are also raising money with fresh stock offerings and IPOs. Meanwhile, China’s GDP has been decelerating and is on pace to undercut its annual target of 4.5%-5%. And while export-facing sectors are growing at a fast clip, trade partners are putting up barriers, Chinese consumers remain reluctant to spend, investment is weak, the property sector is still digging out from an epic crash, and Chinese stocks have been anemic. Beijing has also steered state banks to provide financing to priority industries like electric vehicles, robotics, artificial intelligence and renewable energy. But under pressure to lend, many loans went to questionable borrowers. Business debt has doubled since 2019, while revenues are only 30% higher. Creditors continue to roll over loans to keep struggling firms afloat, even as nearly a third of them are losing money. China’s state-led growth model now looks like it’s running out of steam, and the rapidly expanding mountain of debt is a warning sign as local governments often seek to boost favored industries with low-cost loans. According to the International Monetary Fund , China’s general government gross debt hit 107% of GDP this year, up from 41% in 2015 and on a path to reach 124% in 2030. A broader measure of indebtedness across the public and private sectors reveals an even worse picture. China’s total debt-to-GDP ratio, excluding the financial sector, doubled since 2010 and has now topped 300%, Capital Economics estimated earlier this year. But in the U.S., total public and private debt last year was about 265% of GDP, down sharply from pandemic-era highs. Not only has China’s debt boom hit diminishing returns, but it’s also becoming a drag on the economy. “The irony is that one driver of both government borrowing and the lax lending standards of [state-owned] banks is the desire to prop up economic growth and prevent job losses,” Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics, wrote in May. “But the product of a credit boom that has been underway for 18 years is a banking system propping up unproductive firms, widespread losses across industry, and entrenched overcapacity.” Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

sources.evidenceText: https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/all?displayconttype_exact=Press+Release&lang_exact=English From Higher Revenues to Better Lives: Strengthening State Spending for Growth, Jobs, and Services https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2026/10/08/higher-revenues-better-lives-strengthening-state-spending-for-growth-jobs-services ABUJA, October 8, 2026 — Nigeria’s economic performance has improved in 2026 with a recovery in growth, public finances, and the external position amid a global oil price shock. Sustaining the reform momentum will ensure that the benefits of the reform are widely shared. The reforms led a significant increase in revenue especially to the States. An analysis of where these funds were spent is the special topic of the latest Nigeria Development Update (NDU) titled “Beyond the Federal Purse: How Higher Revenues Reshaped State Priorities.” The report finds that Nigeria’s economy remained resilient, with real GDP growing by 4.2% in the first half of 2026, up from 3.9 and 3.5% in the corresponding periods of 2025 and 2024, respectively. Growth was driven largely by services, alongside a stronger contribution from agriculture. The uptick growth stabilized the poverty rate for the first time since 2019. The conflict in the Middle East has had mixed effects on Nigeria’s economy. Higher oil prices strengthened export earnings and contributed to a larger current account surplus, which rose to $12 billion (7.1% of GDP) in the first half of 2026, up from $8.6 billion (6.7% of GDP) a year earlier. Higher oil prices also boosted fiscal revenues, although the gains were moderated by existing oil pre-commitments under forward sales and oil-backed financing arrangements. Meanwhile, gross external reserves rose above $54 billion in September, supported in large part by foreign portfolio inflows, while ongoing reforms have improved the functioning of the foreign exchange market. At the same time, higher oil prices temporarily stalled the disinflation trend since early 2025. Headline inflation fell sharply from 27.6% in January 2025 to 15.2% in December 2025, supported by tight monetary policy and reduced exchange rate volatility. Higher fuel prices following the onset of the conflict, together with lean season food price pressures, subsequently slowed further progress. Inflation remains elevated and continues to weigh on household purchasing power. The report’s special focus examines how higher public revenues have reshaped state finances and influenced states’ spending priorities. Between 2023 and 2025, gross federation revenues increased by 69% in real terms largely reflecting exchange-rate reforms, the removal of the petrol subsidy, and stronger revenue administration. States recorded the largest increase in federation revenue flows, benefiting not only from higher statutory allocations but also from refunds and the settlement of longstanding federal obligations, dedicated intervention funds, and stronger VAT collections. States used additional fiscal space to expand spending on economic infrastructure and strengthen their fiscal positions. Aggregate state revenues rose by about 93% in real terms between 2023 and 2025 (2019 constant prices), while expenditures rose by about 92% over the same period. Capital spending increased, with its share in total expenditure rising from 46% to 61%. Transport infrastructure accounted for the largest increase, alongside substantial increases in spending on housing, agriculture, and other growth-enhancing investments. Spending on health, education, and social protection also rose substantially but grew more slowly than spending on economic infrastructure. Education’s share of total expenditure declined from 14.9% in 2021 to 12.1% in 2025, while health spending remained broadly stable at around 7%. Social protection’s share increased from 1.4% to 4.4% over the same period. This underscores the opportunity to invest in human capital and service delivery to support the creation of more and better jobs. "The bold macroeconomic reforms have substantially increased fiscal revenues at the state level, providing a unique opportunity to improve infrastructure, education, healthcare, and water services, which are critical to creating more and better jobs. Strengthening spending efficiency, accountability, and service delivery will be essential to ensuring that public resources improve the lives of Nigerians." said Mathew Verghis, World Bank Country Director for Nigeria . States have made significant efforts to enhance fiscal reporting and transparency in recent years, as well as expanding internally generated revenue (IGR). Measures to improve the efficiency of spending and strengthen internally generated revenue will be important next steps for States. The NDU projects that Nigeria’s economy will grow by an average of 4.4% between 2026 and 2028, while inflation is expected to decline gradually to about 12% by 2028 and poverty will start to gradually decline. Sustaining macroeconomic reforms, improving public service delivery, and creating conditions for private sector-led growth and job creation will be essential to faster progress in improving living standards and reducing poverty across the country.

Nigeria is spending more than ₦20 trillion each year on debt servicing, Finance Minister and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has revealed. Speaking in Abuja, Oyedele highlighted that the country’s rising debt-service bill is crowding out funding for essential infrastructure, healthcare, education, and other development needs. Oyedele explained that debt-servicing costs—covering both domestic and foreign obligations—have soared due to high interest rates, themselves a result of monetary tightening aimed at curbing inflation. “Before the reforms, we were borrowing at 8 per cent. It got to 24 per cent,” Oyedele noted. “The amount of money we are using to pay debt service is because we had to raise interest rates to fight inflation.” This debt burden, Oyedele said, exposes a core vulnerability: even with a manageable debt-to-GDP ratio, high servicing costs sharply restrict the government’s ability to fund development. The IMF’s 2026 assessment projects that Nigeria’s interest payments will consume 53.7 per cent of federal revenue this year, up from 53.2 per cent in 2025 and 40.8 per cent in 2024. In practical terms, more than half of government revenue will go to interest payments before accounting for salaries, infrastructure, security, and social services. This trend has serious implications for Nigeria’s fiscal space. As debt service eats up revenue, less is available for capital projects and social spending. The government may have to borrow more to finance deficits, yet higher interest rates make new borrowing even more expensive. According to IMF estimates, Nigeria’s consolidated fiscal deficit will reach 4.7 per cent of GDP in 2026, while public debt is projected at 35.4 per cent of GDP. The real challenge, Oyedele stressed, is not just the debt stock but the proportion of revenue consumed by debt service. Recent Debt Management Office data published on September 25 reflects the continued expansion of both domestic and external debt. Heavy reliance on the domestic debt market exacerbates the problem, as rising yields on government securities push up refinancing costs and crowd out private investment. When banks and pension funds prefer lending to government for higher, safer returns, businesses may face higher borrowing costs, further limiting private sector growth and job creation. Oyedele acknowledged the dilemma: “That’s not the time to say, where do you go for money to build roads, to do healthcare, to do education?” Nigeria’s Eurobond Yields Ease On Rising Investor… Tinubu May Present N54.43trn 2026 Budget Thursday Nigeria’s Public Debt Rises 3.25% to N149.3tr in Q1 2025 He emphasized, however, that borrowing is a normal tool for fiscal management globally. “If government stops borrowing today, this economy will get into a crisis,” he said, citing the U.S. and other advanced economies with large public debts. For Nigeria, the crucial questions are the cost of borrowing, the government’s capacity to generate revenue for debt service, and whether borrowed funds are used for productive investments. Oyedele pointed out that Nigeria’s public expenditure remains low—less than $100 billion for all tiers of government combined—given its population and development needs. He recalled that the Minister of Budget and Economic Planning had also flagged Nigeria’s small budget size, urging that public debate must recognize this fiscal constraint. High debt-service costs only intensify the challenge: every naira devoted to interest payments is unavailable for roads, power, hospitals, or education—unless revenue rises or the country borrows even more. Oyedele noted, though, that much of the interest paid on domestic debt flows back to pension funds and financial institutions, indirectly benefiting retirees and workers. “It’s not going into thin air; it’s going into your pockets,” he said. Still, he warned of the difficult balancing act: high interest rates help contain inflation and attract savings, but they also raise the government’s costs and limit private-sector investment. A sustained reduction in inflation could allow for lower interest rates, easing government borrowing and freeing up funds for development. Since debt servicing is a mandatory obligation, revenue shortfalls typically squeeze discretionary and capital spending instead. Oyedele called for greater public understanding and accountability in fiscal management: “We want you to hold us to account, but to do so with the right knowledge.” Ultimately, Nigeria’s challenge is not whether to borrow, but how to ensure that economic reforms raise revenue, lower inflation and interest rates, and improve the quality and impact of government spending. The International Atomic Energy Agency Board of Governors voted to close the investigation into Syria’s nuclear program after the agency reported that the new Syrian government provided the necessary cooperation to resolve long-standing questions about the illicit nuclear activities of the deposed Assad regime. The Sept. 9 resolution, which passed unanimously, welcomed Syria’s cooperation. It noted that Syria has “taken the measures required to remedy the non-compliance found by the Board” in 2011 and closed the investigation. IAEA Director-General Rafael Mariano Grossi hailed Syria’s cooperation with the agency as a “breakthrough” in a Sept. 7 statement to the board. The government’s transparency and cooperation facilitate “resolution of the outstanding safeguards issues related to Syria’s past nuclear activities,” he said. In a Sept. 14 video statement to the IAEA General Conference, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani expressed gratitude to the IAEA and board for closing the noncompliance case “inherited from the previous regime.” He reaffirmed Syria’s commitment to transparency and IAEA safeguards going forward. Shibani said that Syria offers a “model” for resolving nonproliferation threats in the region and called on all nuclear facilities “without any exception, to be placed under safeguards.” The IAEA was able to resolve its concerns about Syria’s past nuclear activities after the new Syrian government negotiated an access agreement with the IAEA July 29. Before that agreement, Syria notified the agency in a July 17 letter about the discovery of a cache of undeclared nuclear materials dating from when President Bashar al-Assad ruled the country. He was ousted in 2024 by opposition forces. As a result of the information and access provided under the July 29 agreement, the IAEA assessed in a Sept. 1 report that it was able to “establish that the former Syrian authorities had failed to report nuclear material, facilities and activities as required” under the nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty (NPT) safeguards agreement. The report affirmed previous IAEA assessments, which led the Board of Governors to pass a resolution in 2011 that declared Syria in violation of its NPT-required safeguards agreement for constructing a nuclear reactor at Deir el-Zour without informing the agency. The IAEA requested access to the site after Israel bombed it in 2007, but the Assad regime refused to cooperate with the agency, leading to the board’s decision to declare Syria in noncompliance. The Sept. 1 report concluded that Syria took “measures to remedy the situation by providing to the Agency the required nuclear material accounting reports and design information for the above-mentioned facilities in accordance with its NPT Safeguards Agreement.” The IAEA noted 73 tons of natural uranium metal, 55 tons of which are in the form of fuel rods and 18 of which are uranium waste and scrap, when it inspected the newly discovered site. Syria declared the nuclear material to the agency and provided an accountancy report Aug. 27, according to the IAEA report. That material is now under IAEA safeguards in Syria. The agency’s excavations at the Deir el-Zour site confirmed previous assessments that Syria was building an undeclared nuclear reactor at the site. According to the report, the IAEA uncovered “cooling infrastructure” that is “consistent with that of a nuclear reactor.” The Sept. 1 report also noted that agency inspectors visited three locations connected to Deir el-Zour, including a facility intended for fabricating fuel for the reactor. The IAEA visited those sites in 2024 to take environmental samples, which tested positive for uranium. Despite the closure of the investigation, the Sept. 9 resolution requested that the IAEA director-general provide an update about the agency’s ongoing activities in Syria “upon their completion.” In a Sept. 10 speech, the U.S. ambassador to the IAEA, Wells Griffith III, called the adoption of the resolution a “historic milestone” but noted that the “work of Syria and the IAEA is not yet complete.” He said that “many questions related to Assad’s program remain unanswered” and requested a “detailed assessment of Syria’s previously undeclared nuclear program” from Grossi. Griffith called on Syria to sign an additional protocol—giving the IAEA expanded access to sites and more tools to verify that a state’s nuclear program is entirely peaceful—to its safeguards agreement “as early as possible.” Adopting an additional protocol “would be an important demonstration of the Syrian government’s enduring commitment to transparency and to fostering international trust,” he said.— The Arms Control Association depends on the generous contributions of individuals who share our goal of promoting public understanding of and support for effective arms control policies. sources.evidenceText: GAZA: One year after a US-brokered ceasefire was announced in the Gaza Strip, residents still living in displacement camps under near-daily Israeli airstrikes say the truce has not brought the promised peace. Israel keeps up its strikes and now controls about 70 percent of Gaza, while the reconstruction of the devastated Palestinian territory called for under the ceasefire plan has still not materialized. “Nothing has changed for the better; everything has gotten worse, they lie to us, it is all lies,” said Fatima Awkal, a displaced woman in Gaza City. “Martyrs are still falling, people are still being injured, the shelling continues, and we cannot even find a moment’s peace from the constant buzzing of the drones overhead.” On the streets of Gaza City, rows of white tents line passageways that have been cleared of rubble from destroyed homes, while in the distance blown-out windows gape from the facades of buildings that remain standing. Ahmed Jonaid, another displaced Palestinian in Gaza City, said he had hoped to return home after the ceasefire. “We thought we would experience some happiness and return to our homes. Instead, we see ourselves suffering in refugee camps, sleeping on makeshift mats,” the 51-year-old said as he carried two jerricans of water back to his tent. Almost all of Gaza’s more than 2 million residents were displaced at least once during the war that broke out with the attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. With 82 percent of all standing structures in Gaza either damaged or destroyed as of mid-2026, per the UN, many residents still live in tents or makeshift shelters, where overcrowding and a lack of hygiene have led to outbreaks of disease. Ahmed Shawan, a doctor at a hospital in the southern city of Khan Yunis, said that he had yet to see the ceasefire take effect on the ground. “It has been a full year since the ceasefire was declared, yet it exists only on paper,” he said. sources.evidenceText: Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on. Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region. The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces. The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war. However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea. So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war? Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty. In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”. He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking. Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive. Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”. He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”. The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea. Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea. Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”. “The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera. Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years. Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts. “Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera. He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said. “The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.” Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions. The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city. In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force. Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi. It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting. Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified. The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement. That conflict began in November 2020 after months of tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018. Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF, its longtime adversary. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger. The November 2022 Pretoria agreement ended major hostilities, but Eritrea was not a party to the deal. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara subsequently deteriorate

sources.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea edge closer to direct conflict as troops enter Tigray | The National
sources.imageAlt: A vehicle of the Ethiopian National Defence Force patrols the streets of Mekelle, after seizing control of the capital of the Tigray region at the weekend. AFP
sources.evidenceText: Eritrean troops have crossed into Ethiopia 's Tigray region and come under fire from Ethiopian drones as they pushed south, a conflict monitor said. It is the clearest sign yet that Ethiopia's renewed internal troubles could spark a war between the two neighbours. Eritrean troops have crossed the border at the town of Zalambessa and headed for the road between Adigrat and Idaga Hamus, said Dr Jalale Getachew Birru, East Africa analyst at the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled). “Ethiopian National Defence Forces drones targeted Eritrean troops at Guada as they travelled by vehicle towards Idaga Hamus,” he said. Residents of Adigrat, about 25km south of the border, told Reuters they saw two military vehicles carrying dozens of Eritrean soldiers pass through the town on Wednesday morning. Ethiopia demanded that the troops leave. “All foreign military forces operating within our sovereign territory must withdraw immediately,” said Enatalem Melese, Government Communication Minister. Eritrea did not deny its troops had crossed the border. In a post on X, Information Minister Yemane Meskel on Wednesday accused Ethiopia of building “a fallacious narrative of 'self defence' to rationalise and camouflage its war of aggression”. The crossing into Ethiopia comes days after federal forces retook Mekelle, the Tigrayan capital, from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). According to Acled data, Tigray Defence Forces, the TPLF's armed wing, have a heavy presence in Idaga Hamus and Adigrat. Many TPLF leaders are in the rural Ahferom district of central Tigray, Dr Jalale said. He said Eritrea is suspected of backing the Alliance for Survival, a coalition of seven armed groups, including the TPLF, that was formed last month to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. Eritrea has two possible motives, he said. It was unhappy with the 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the war in Tigray, because it wanted the TPLF destroyed. Asmara's grievances against the TPLF date back to the 1998-2000 border war, when the party led Ethiopia. Dr Jalale said it wants to turn Tigray into a buffer zone that is hostile to Addis Ababa. “Hence, Eritrean forces entered the war in Tigray to halt the Ethiopian government and allied forces from reaching the border and potentially fighting within Eritrea's territory,” he said. The commander of the pro-government Tigray Peace Force, Gebreigziabher Beyene, made a similar point. Eritrea is “deliberately deploying its forces so that the fighting takes place inside Tigray rather than spilling into Eritrea”, he told AFP. Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara last Thursday and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats, accusing them of threatening national security. Eritrea responded by cutting ties. The US has warned that “the Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis”. In a statement on Saturday, it urged both countries to exercise “maximum restraint”. Eritrea's move also puts the spotlight on Egypt, which has its own dispute with Ethiopia over its share of the Nile, in addition to the latter's Red Sea ambitions. Cairo has spent the past few years building ties with Asmara. In October 2024, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi and his Eritrean counterpart Isaias Afwerki agreed with Somalia's President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud on a framework for strategic co-operation that includes Red Sea security. Ahmed Moussa, a prominent pro-government Egyptian television host, said on Saturday that Egypt and Eritrea have a joint defence agreement, though no text has ever been made public. With Cairo and Addis Ababa trading blame over the Nile dam and also expelling each other's diplomats last week, the question now is how far Egypt would go if its ally faces a serious Ethiopian attack.
