sources.evidenceText: Islamabad — Key Saudi ally Pakistan has confirmed it has troops stationed in the Gulf kingdom, as Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen continue cross-border attacks with deadly assaults on airports. “The forces of Pakistan are already there. That I can share with you,” Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told CNN in an exclusive interview on Wednesday, without specifying how many or their capabilities, saying those details were classified. The confirmation from Chaudhry, the chief of the Pakistani military’s media wing, came just days after the two nations and Turkey agreed to the rapid deployment of the forces, as part of a newly minted mutual defense treaty. Over the past two days, the Houthis have killed three people in attacks on Saudi’s Abha International Airport, near the Yemen border, and King Khalid International Airport, in the capital Riyadh, Saudi officials said. The attacks underscore how the conflict is increasingly affecting Saudi territory as Riyadh deepens its support for the Yemeni government’s military campaign. The targeting of the airports prompted an updated security alert from the US Mission in Saudi Arabia, warning American citizens the conflict “has the potential to escalate.” The Iran-backed Houthis, who control much of northern Yemen including the capital, Sanaa, have been at war with the internationally recognized Yemeni government and a Saudi-led coalition since 2015. The conflict flared up in July, shortly after the US-Iran ceasefire unravelled, with Houthi missile attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in an expansion of the Middle East war. Riyadh has responded with airstrikes in support of Yemeni government forces. In recent days, Yemeni government forces have claimed advances near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, which the Houthis claimed effective control of last month. The Houthis have responded with missile and drone attacks against targets inside Saudi Arabia. Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco, south of Riyadh, on October 3, 2026. In recent weeks Aramco, majority-owned by the Saudi state, has come under attack from the Houthi authorities targeting the kingdom as part of the war in Yemen. AFP/Getty Images Pakistan’s troops in Saudi The escalation has coincided with Saudi moves to strengthen defense cooperation with regional military heavyweights Turkey, a NATO member, and nuclear-armed Pakistan The trio recently signed a pact with NATO-style collective defense provisions, often referred to as the Mecca Alliance. The deployment of Pakistani forces had “not come out of a vacuum” Chaudhry, Director General of the Inter-Services Public Relations, told CNN. Pakistan has had a military presence in Saudi Arabia for decades, he said. Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi’s security was “absolute,” Chaudhry said. He described the alliance as a mechanism for collective defense under which an attack on one member would be considered an attack on all. But he would not be drawn on whether Pakistani troops would be involved in any operations across the border in Yemen. “Whenever there is a military conflict, no participating country starts disclosing how and where it is going to employ its forces,” he said, adding the any involvement would be “defensive in nature.” “The objective of this alliance is not to start labelling enemies, enemies, enemies, friends, friends, friends. The objective is the defense of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia… That will be done,” said Chaudhry. In a joint statement following an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday, the three countries said they would move immediately to implement collective defense commitments and ensure the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Chaudhry said the collective security agreement would also act as a deterrent. “Anyone having some funny ideas against another will hopefully think twice, thrice, or multiple times before doing that. sources.evidenceText: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan has confirmed that its soldiers are already stationed in Saudi Arabia, days after Riyadh, Islamabad and Ankara activated a new three-way defence pact in response to escalating attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels. Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the Pakistani military’s media wing, made the admission in an interview with CNN’s Ivan Watson. “I can confirm that the forces of Pakistan are already there,” Lt Gen Chaudhry said. Asked whether troops were on the ground under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, he said Pakistani personnel had been in the kingdom for far longer than the pact has existed. “Pakistan troops have been there for decades,” he said. “The Makkah alliance is not something that has come out in a vacuum.” He added: “There is a sustained diplomatic, political, military and people-to-people relationship between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia. So, I can share with you that Pakistani forces, in multiple capabilities and domains, are already there.” The comments follow an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday of the alliance’s Strategic Political and Defence Committee. It was the first time the alliance has been invoked since it was signed on 7 August. A Pakistani Foreign Office statement said the committee had decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of its collective defence commitments. It said the three countries would provide the agreed forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom, in line with approved arrangements and each country’s national laws. It did not name a specific threat or say what the troops would do. Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, said on X that the committee had agreed to activate collective deterrence measures in response to the attacks and those responsible for them. The meeting also condemned the attempted targeting of the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The committee also appointed a retired Pakistani general, Nauman Mahmood, as the alliance’s first secretary general for a three-year term, according to the Foreign Office. Pakistan’s defence minister, Khawaja Asif, part of the delegation in Riyadh, told a private television channel the same day that Saudi forces had made gains and recovered some areas in Yemen. Asked about a possible operational role for Pakistan and Turkey, he said both had a “presence in theatre”, but that only Saudi troops were involved in combat. “Whatever assistance they require is being provided,” Asif said. “But right now, the Turkish and Pakistani armies are playing a supportive role.” He said Pakistan was involved in reconnaissance. He had earlier said Pakistan would stand by Saudi Arabia “practically and diplomatically” if the situation escalated, and would meet all its obligations under the alliance. The pact commits its members to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. On 25 September the military chiefs of the three countries met in Riyadh for urgent talks under its terms. A week earlier Lt Gen Chaudhry had said Pakistan would go to “any extent” to defend the kingdom and that its commitment was “unconditional”. Pakistan’s military presence in Saudi Arabia is long established, and has included training and advisory deployments. Riyadh has repeatedly supported Islamabad financially in periods of economic stress. The two countries also signed a separate bilateral defence agreement last September. Reuters reported in May that Islamabad had sent 8,000 troops, a squadron of fighter jets and an air defence system to the kingdom under that deal. Turkey is also sending Saudi Arabia mainly defensive and technical support, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing two officials. Ankara, which has NATO’s second-largest army, has condemned the Houthi attacks. It has also agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea. The alliance’s activation comes as the fighting in and around Yemen sharpens. The Houthis have fired missiles and drones at Saudi targets since late July, hitting industrial and energy infrastructure. Their attacks ended a 2022 truce that had largely halted fighting with the Saudi-led coalition. On Sunday, Yemen’s internationally recognised government announced a major campaign to recapture all territory held by the Houthis. The Houthis said they had hit Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area. The coalition’s spokesman called the claims “misleading”, and Saudi Arabia did not immediately confirm any attack. On Monday the Houthis went further, claiming strikes on Riyadh’s international airport and an Aramco refinery. That claim has not been independently verified. sources.evidenceText: DHAKA, Bangladesh — Eight-month-old Rojatun Jannat Ramisa is struggling to breathe in a hospital in Bangladesh’s capital as her parents sit helplessly beside her. She is one of thousands of children sickened by a measles outbreak that is sweeping across the South Asian country and has killed hundreds of children following setbacks to the national vaccine program. Ramisa’s mother, Ranu Akhter, traveled hundreds of miles after doctors in eastern Bangladesh referred her to a specialized child hospital in Dhaka to seek treatment for the life-threatening condition. “Fourteen days ago, when we were at the district hospital, there were other children being treated alongside my daughter. I saw that those children also had red rashes on their bodies, sores in their mouths and fevers,” Akhter told The Associated Press at Dhaka Shishu Hospital. “It made me realize how widespread the measles outbreak is,” she said. Every day, the death toll is rising. Bangladesh has been racing to halt the outbreak’s spread since March, when more than 100 children died in less than a month. By Tuesday, the death toll from suspected measles cases reached 999 since the start of the year, according to the government’s Directorate General of Health Services. Since March, the country has recorded more than 166,000 suspected measles cases, including 19,835 laboratory-confirmed infections, according to the Ministry of Health. The government launched an emergency vaccination drive in March together with the World Health Organization, the U.N. children’s agency and the Gavi vaccine alliance. It began with a focus on children from 6 months to 5 years old and later expanded nationwide in phases. Measles is a highly contagious airborne disease that causes fever, respiratory symptoms and a characteristic rash. It can sometimes have severe or fatal complications, especially in young children, according to the WHO. Two doses of a vaccine provide strong protection against measles, but the WHO says 95% of the population has to be vaccinated in order to stop the disease from spreading — which protects children like Ramisa who are too young to be vaccinated as well as immunocompromised people. About 86% of children in Bangladesh got their recommended second dose of measles vaccine last year, according to an estimate by the World Health Organization and UNICEF. That’s down from 93% in 2024. A few years ago, Bangladesh had measles largely under control, with a vaccination program that was credited for decades for protecting children and mothers from the deadly diseases of tuberculosis, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, poliomyelitis and measles. From 2021 to 2025, the country recorded just 100 to 300 cases per year, down from 2,410 cases in 2020. But in the last few years, disruptions to the vaccine program have left a growing number of children unvaccinated. First the Covid-19 pandemic interrupted routine vaccinations, and then in 2024 the government largely missed a vaccination campaign previously carried out every four years. Atiqul Islam, a neonatal and child specialist at Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, said that during the pandemic period in 2021 and 2022, many parents did not take their children to get vaccinated. “So, if you look at children who are now 4 or 5 years old, many of them missed their vaccinations. That created a gap. During the previous interim government, vaccines were also unavailable at many vaccination centers,” he said. Bangladesh’s current government, headed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, said the failures in planning under ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and interim leader Muhammad Yunus left the country with shortages of vaccines and far behind on coverage. The 2024 measles vaccination campaign was disrupted during the political upheaval that led to Hasina’s ouster. She left the country in the face of a mass uprising in August 2024, and was followed by Yunus, who led an interim administration that transferred power to an elected government after an election in February. From exile in India, Hasina blamed the Yunus-led government for the disaster. At Bangladesh Shishu Hospital, Islam said the situation has improved, but not enough. Privacy On 6 October 2026 the Canary Islands health authority confirmed the detection of Aedes aegypti larvae in a flat in the centre of Mogán. The investigation was triggered by a report of unusual mosquito bites from a person who contacted the surveillance system. Specialists from the Institute of Tropical Diseases and Public Health of the University of La Laguna (IUETSPC-ULL) and the Gran Canaria health area inspected the property. The medical entomology laboratory of the IUETSPC-ULL identified the larvae as Aedes aegypti, the yellow fever mosquito. Adult specimens of the invasive species Aedes albopictus, the tiger mosquito, had already been confirmed in Motor Grande on 1 October 2026. The two locations are in different parts of the same municipality. This is the first time that both invasive Aedes species have been recorded in a single municipality in the Canary Islands. The detection of the mosquitoes does not mean that dengue, chikungunya or Zika viruses are present in Mogán. Both species can transmit various arboviruses, including dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses. According to the Director-General for Public Health, José Díaz Flores, an Aedes mosquito can bite 30 to 40 times per hour and cause severe swelling. The health authority says the tiger mosquito bites mainly during the day, especially at dawn and dusk. According to the Directorate-General for Public Health, 24 episodes of invasive mosquitoes have been recorded in the Canary Islands since 2017. The authorities say they have so far been controlled through early detection and rapid action. The health authority has activated the surveillance protocol. Several types of traps have been placed in the flat and its surroundings, and inspections and sampling have been stepped up. The aim is to establish the spatial spread. For the Aedes albopictus detection site, the protocol provides for additional traps, more frequent sampling and cleaning and fumigation work. In the case of Aedes aegypti detections, investigation areas with radii of 200 and 500 metres are also set up. Public Health, the University of La Laguna and the Ayuntamiento de Mogán (municipal council) are coordinating cleaning, control and information work. This includes epidemiological surveys, the removal of possible breeding sites and, where infestation is confirmed, treatment of the affected buildings. The health authority recommends removing standing water and turning over empty containers outdoors. According to the authority, even a bottle cap can become a breeding site, because the females need small accumulations of water for their larvae to develop. Plant pot saucers should be filled with sand or emptied and cleaned weekly. Water in vases and animal drinking bowls should be changed daily. Water containers should be covered. Swimming pools should be chlorinated and the water circulated daily. Cleaning drains and air-conditioning drip trays also helps to prevent breeding. Suspected mosquitoes or unusually severe reactions to bites can be reported with a photo, location and telephone number to [email protected] . It is not yet clear how Aedes aegypti reached Mogán. The authorities are investigating a possibly isolated, accidental introduction through materials that could contain eggs. No exact completion or all-clear date has been published. Additional traps, more frequent checks and the analysis of samples should first show whether the mosquito has spread beyond the property affected so far. The reports of bites and mosquitoes received so far for Aedes aegypti are limited to the property that triggered the investigation. The Canary Islands entomological surveillance system has been in place at ports and airports since 2013. According to the available official information, there are no announced closures, travel bans, new charges or special entry requirements for Mogán. The current episodes in Mogán remain surveillance cases. Permanent establishment has not been confirmed. The authorities stress that the 24 episodes recorded since 2017 have so far been controlled.
